title: Authorization boundary mapping and decision points
content:
Summary:

Working notes on where we should draw authorization boundaries across the routing stack for Redwood Inference (edge, control plane, runtime) and where policy decisions (PDP) should live. Goal: minimize blast radius, keep latency within SLOs, preserve auditability and comply with region-local constraints. This is a practical mapping + rollout checklist rather than a formal spec.

Context and assumptions:
- Multi-region deployments: control plane may be centralized (us-east) or region-local depending on product tier (hosted vs dedicated vs private).
- We have three main traffic surfaces: external API ingress (edge/API gateways), control plane (management/config APIs), and runtime inference plane (model servers / envoys).
- Two broad policy types: 1) coarse-grained access control (who can call which APIs or manage resources) and 2) fine-grained request-level runtime policy (per-request data policies, customer-specific routing, quota checks).

High-level boundary proposal (recommended):
1) Edge / API gateway (first enforcement layer)
   - Responsibilities: authentication (JWT/OIDC/OAuth), token validation, coarse RBAC checks for public API routes, early reject for malformed/expired tokens, rate-limiting and global quotas.
   - Implementation: Envoy filter / ingress sidecar that validates signatures and extracts attributes (org-id, user-id, tier, region).
   - Why here: cheap to reject unauthorized traffic early, prevents hammering downstream PDPs, enforces global quotas close to client.

2) Control plane policy service (PDP) — authoritative decision maker for config & admin actions
   - Responsibilities: admin RBAC, resource-level authorization (create/destroy model deployments, change routing policies), policy authoring UI, audit trails for config changes.
   - Placement: central control plane with region-aware caches for read-heavy operations in dedicated/private deployments.
   - Notes: Control-plane policy decisions can be cached at edge for short TTLs when safe.

3) Runtime / Serving enforcement points (PIP + enforcement hooks)
   - Responsibilities: per-request ABAC decisions that depend on runtime attributes (prompt content, session KV, model variant compatibility, customer-configured safety policies), enforcement of data residency for certain customers, per-tenant quotas at token-level, canary rollouts and fallback routing.
   - Implementation: lightweight authz hooks inside the serving runtime (inference front-proxy), with a fast local PDP for high-QPS checks and async auditing to control plane.
   - Why here: runtime attributes only available at serving time (sequence lengths, model cache state, KV cache hits, attached tools), and routing decisions (which model variant / fallback) must be made in the request path.

Design patterns and components
- PDP vs PEP vs PAP vs PIP: we keep the PDP (policy decision point) concept central but accept multiple co-located PDPS: a master PDP in the control plane (authoritative) and lightweight regional PDPS embedded in the runtime for low-latency checks. PEPs (policy enforcement points) live at ingress and in the runtime proxy. PAP (policy administration) is the console + API. PIP (policy information point) is the attribute source (user profile service, tenant configs, runtime metrics).

- Hybrid ABAC/RBAC model:
  - RBAC: use for control-plane/admin operations and for coarse route gating (internal roles, operator actions). Stable, low-cardinality, easy to audit.
  - ABAC: use for request-level decisions in the runtime (attributes: tenant tier, model family, request purpose, content flags, location). ABAC supports dynamic rules (e.g., deny high-context-length requests for tier-free).
  - Hybrid rules can be expressed as RBAC + attribute constraints in the policy language.

Latency & caching strategy
- Decision latency budget: for runtime routing decisions target < 5 ms extra p99 to keep overall infer latency SLOs intact.
- Cache short-lived decisions at the PEP with TTLs derived from attribute stability (e.g., token->role TTL = token expiry; tenant-level policy TTL = 30s by default).
- Use local PDPS with warm-up streams and an eventual-consistent policy sync from control plane. Policy sync should be incremental with content addressing or version stamps.

Failure modes and fallback policies
- PDP unreachable: enforce configurable fallback behaviors per tenant and route. Options: fail-open (allow) for read-only endpoints, fail-closed (deny) for admin/deploy ops, conservative default for runtime inference should prefer availability with reduced feature set (e.g., route to a safe baseline model variant).
- Stale policy: add policy version in decision logs and surface alerts if runtime version diverges from control plane by > N minutes.
- Partial enforcement: when some attributes unavailable (PIP unreachable), treat absent attributes as unknown and let policy rules specify default. Avoid surprise wide-open defaults.

Auditability & compliance
- Every decision must emit an audit event: timestamp, request id, signing key id, PDP version, decision (allow/deny), applied rule id, attributes used. These should be written asynchronously to region-local audit store and replicated to central audit for long-term retention.
- For regulated customers requiring data locality, enforce that both decision path and audit storage remain inside allowed region. Policy service must be deployable in private-mode with local persistence.

Operational concerns
- Rollout testing: golden traffic tests for policy changes; staged rollout with canaries; automated regression checks using historical request traces and sample prompts.
- Observability: per-route authz latency histograms, cache hit rates, PDP error rates, decision variance across regions. Create alert when authz contributes > 10% of p99 request latency.
- Key management: token signature keys and policy signing keys stored in KMS/HSM; signed policy bundles enable atomic updates and allow runtime to verify origin.

Example request decision flow (simplified):
1) Client -> Edge Envoy filter verifies JWT signature (OIDC), extracts tenant_id, user_id, roles, region_hint.
2) Edge does a quick RBAC check for route-level allow/deny (cached). If denied -> reject.
3) If allowed and request is inference, forward with attributes to runtime proxy. Runtime PEP consults local PDP for ABAC decision (model access, data residency) with cached policy version.
4) PDP returns decision + optional routing instruction (route_to: model-v2, fallback: model-safe). Runtime enforces decision and logs audit to local store.
5) Async: runtime replicates decision summary to central audit and increments quota counters in a distributed counter service.

Checklist for implementation (minimum viable):
- [ ] Edge JWT validation + route-level RBAC filters (Envoy).
- [ ] Control-plane policy authoring and versioned bundles (signed).
- [ ] Lightweight regional PDP library for runtime with plumbing for incremental policy updates.
- [ ] Common policy language (rule ids, attribute model, de-duplication strategy).
- [ ] Audit sink connectors (region-local + central replication).
- [ ] Fallback policy configurations with tenant overrides.
- [ ] Load-testing harness for authz latency at p99 under realistic QPS.

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
- How aggressively do we cache per-request decisions vs risk of policy drift? (tunable per-tenant)
- Single authoritative PDP vs multi-master replicas for private deployments? (prefer master-control-plane with region-local read-replicas)
- Should policy language support embedded rate-limit semantics or keep rate limits as separate quota service? (separate service simplifies audit / counters)
- For on-prem/private, do we enforce cryptographic policy bundle signatures or trust the local admin? (signing recommended for hybrid setups)

Immediate next steps:
- Sync with runtime team to spec the lightweight PDP API (check/decision protos) and perf targets. Owner: Miguel Santos.
- Draft a small policy catalog (RBAC entries for admin workflows, ABAC samples for tenant quotas and model gating). Owner: Hannah Lee.
- Put together a short chaos plan for PDP outage modes and a demo that shows fail-open vs fail-closed behavior. Owner: Jon Park.

Notes to self / todo reminders:
- Add example policy snippets (Rego or custom DSL) in a follow-up doc.
- Coordinate with privacy team on audit retention defaults per region.
- Add a one-pager for solutions engineering on tenant-level overrides for Dedicated customers.

End.
